moduleMetadata.title: Password & Account Security
moduleMetadata.description: Learn how to create strong passwords, use security tools effectively, and protect your accounts from unauthorized access.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Your online accounts are often the gateway to your personal information, academic records, communications, files, and other digital resources. An attacker does not always need to break into a complicated system. Sometimes, obtaining or guessing a user's password is enough.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users should understand how to create and maintain stronger and more secure accounts.

learningObjectives: Distinguish between strong and weak passwords.
Apply password length and complexity principles.
Understand the risks of password reuse.
Use password managers and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
Recognize signs of account takeover and credential theft.

sections.title: 1. What Is a Password?
sections.content: A password is a secret used to authenticate a user and help prove that they are authorized to access an account or system. A password is only useful as a security control if it is difficult for unauthorized people to discover or obtain.

sections.title: 2. Strong vs Weak Passwords
sections.content: A weak password is easy to guess, predict, or obtain. A stronger password is more difficult to guess and is unique to the account.
bulletPoints: Avoid your name, birthday, phone number, university name, favorite team, family member's name, simple sequences, common words, and repeated characters.
Weak patterns include password123, 12345678, qwerty123, and Ali2007.
Do not use these examples as actual passwords.
sections.callout: A password should be difficult for unauthorized people to discover or obtain.

sections.title: 3. Password Length Matters
sections.content: One of the most important characteristics of a password is length. In general, longer passwords provide more possible combinations and can be harder to guess.

subsections.title: Compare the concepts
subsections.content:
Short password: Tiger7

Longer passphrase: river-lamp-coffee-window

The second example is much longer and can be easier for a person to remember while providing more possible combinations.

sections.callout: Length is a major part of password strength. Do not focus only on adding one symbol or changing one letter.

sections.title: 4. Password Complexity
sections.content: Password complexity can involve:

subsections.title: Explanation
subsections.content:
However, simply adding a number or symbol to a common password does not automatically make it secure.

For example, changing:

password

to:

Password1!

still follows a very common and predictable pattern.

subsections.title: Better Principle
subsections.content:
Think about:

Length + Uniqueness + Unpredictability

rather than complexity alone.

sections.title: 5. Password Reuse
sections.content: Password reuse means using the same password on multiple accounts. If the password is exposed from one service, an attacker may attempt to use it on your other accounts. This can turn one compromised account into several compromised accounts.
sections.callout: One important account = One unique password. Your most important accounts should never depend on the same password.

sections.title: 6. Common Password Mistakes
sections.content: Users commonly make mistakes that make account compromise easier.
bulletPoints: Using personal information such as a name, birthday, phone number, or address.
Using common passwords that appear in attacker password lists.
Sharing passwords with friends, classmates, colleagues, or other people.
Writing passwords in visible or unsecured locations.
Using predictable patterns such as Password1, Password2, and Password3.
sections.callout: Changing only a number does not provide meaningful separation between passwords.

sections.title: 7. Password Managers
sections.content: A password manager is a tool designed to securely store and manage passwords. Instead of remembering dozens of unique passwords, a user can use a password manager to help manage them.

subsections.title: Important principle
subsections.content: You still need to protect the password manager itself. Use strong protection for the password manager and enable MFA where supported.

sections.title: 8. Multi-Factor Authentication
sections.content: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) adds another layer of verification to an account. Instead of relying only on a password, MFA requires an additional authentication factor.
factors: Something You Know — password or PIN
Something You Have — phone, authentication device, or security key
Something You Are — fingerprint or face recognition

sections.title: 9. Why MFA Matters
sections.content: If an attacker obtains your password, the additional factor can make unauthorized access more difficult. Without MFA, a password may be enough for account access. With MFA, the attacker must also complete the additional verification step.
sections.callout: Never share authentication codes with someone who unexpectedly asks for them.

sections.title: 10. Protecting Your MFA
sections.content: MFA improves security, but users still need to protect their authentication factors.

subsections.title: Unexpected MFA request
subsections.content: If someone calls claiming to be IT and asks for the code that just appeared on your phone, do not provide the code and independently verify the request.

sections.callout: Unexpected MFA request = Stop and verify.

sections.title: 11. Account Takeover
sections.content: An account takeover occurs when an unauthorized person gains control of someone else's account.

subsections.title: What an attacker may do
subsections.content: Change account settings or the password; access private information or stored files; send fraudulent messages; attack other accounts; and lock the legitimate user out.

sections.title: 12. Warning Signs of Account Takeover
sections.content: Possible warning signs include:
checklist: Login alerts you do not recognize
Password-reset emails you did not request
Messages sent from your account that you did not send
Changes to account settings you did not make
Unknown devices appearing in account activity

subsections.title: What should you do?
subsections.content: Stop interacting with suspicious messages. Use the official account or service website. Change the password if appropriate, enable MFA, review account activity and sessions, follow the service's account-recovery process, and report the incident when necessary.

sections.title: 13. Credential Theft
sections.content: Credentials are information used to authenticate a user. Credential theft occurs when an attacker obtains authentication information without authorization.

sections.title: 14. Fake Login Pages
sections.content: A credential thief may create a website that looks similar to a legitimate email provider or other service. The victim enters a username and password, and the information may be sent to the attacker.
sections.callout: Do not trust a login page simply because it looks professional.

sections.title: 15. Password Reset Scams
sections.content: Attackers may use fake password-reset messages, such as: "A password reset has been requested for your account. Click immediately to cancel it." The message may contain a malicious link.
bulletPoints: You did not request a reset.
The link goes to an unexpected domain.
Someone asks for your password or MFA code.
Someone asks you to approve an unexpected login.

subsections.title: Safer approach
subsections.content: Do not use the suspicious link. Open the official service directly, check your account security, and use the official password-reset process.

sections.title: 16. Protecting Important Accounts
sections.content: Some accounts can provide access to many other services.
sections.callout: Your primary email may be connected to password-reset systems for other accounts. Protect your primary email like a master key.

sections.title: 17. Account Security Checklist
sections.content: Before considering an important account well protected, ask:
checklist: Do I use a unique password?
Have I checked recent login activity?
Do I recognize the devices connected to the account?
Do I know how to report or recover a compromised account?
sections.callout: The more important the account, the more seriously you should treat these questions.

sections.title: 18. Interactive Tool — Password Strength Checker
sections.content: MilcharSec can provide a Password Strength Checker as an interactive learning tool. Its purpose is to teach users what makes passwords stronger or weaker.
bulletPoints: Password length — longer passwords generally provide more possible combinations.
Repeated patterns — repeated characters or predictable sequences can reduce strength; for example, aaaa1111.
Common password patterns — such as Password123.
Predictability — passwords based on easily guessed information can receive a lower assessment.
Overall feedback — Weak, Moderate, Strong, or Very Strong.
sections.callout: The goal is not simply to give a score, but to explain why a password receives that assessment.

sections.title: 19. Privacy Rule for the Password Checker
sections.content: A password-strength learning tool should be designed with privacy in mind.

subsections.title: Important security requirement
subsections.content: The system should not permanently store user passwords. Ideally, it should evaluate the password locally or process it temporarily without retaining the original password.

subsections.title: Never use a real password
subsections.content: For training purposes, learners should use a fictional test password, such as Training-Example-Only-2026!, not a password they actually use.

sections.title: 20. Interactive Challenge — Build a Better Account
sections.content: You are creating a new university account. Which approach is safest? A. Use the same password as your social media account. B. Use your name and birthday. C. Create a unique password and enable MFA. D. Share the password with your closest friend in case you forget it.
sections.callout: Correct answer: C — Create a unique password and enable MFA.

sections.title: 21. Interactive Challenge — Spot the Scam
sections.content: You receive this message: "Your university account will be deleted today. Send us your password and MFA code immediately to prevent account closure."
sections.callout: Correct answer: All of the above. Do not provide the credentials; verify the message through an official university channel.

sections.title: 22. Scenario — Unexpected Login
sections.content: You receive an alert: "New login detected from an unfamiliar device." You do not recognize the login.

subsections.title: What should you do?
subsections.content: Investigate through the official account security page and secure the account if necessary. Do not reply to the alert or share it with friends.

sections.callout: Correct answer: C — Investigate through the official account security page and secure the account if necessary.

sections.title: 23. Knowledge Quiz
sections.content: This module's knowledge check covers password strength, password reuse, password managers, MFA, account takeover, and protecting the primary email account.

sections.title: 24. Final Challenge — Secure the Account
sections.content: Choose SAFE, SUSPICIOUS, or REPORT for each situation.
bulletPoints: Create a unique password for a university account and enable MFA — SAFE.
A message asks you to send your password so support can verify your identity — SUSPICIOUS.
Receive an unexpected MFA approval request you did not initiate — REPORT.
Use the same password for email, university, and social media — SUSPICIOUS.
Use a fictional password in the Password Strength Checker — SAFE.

sections.title: 25. Key Takeaways
sections.content: By completing this module, you should understand that:
bulletPoints: Strong account security starts with long, unique, and unpredictable passwords.
Password reuse can allow one exposed password to affect multiple accounts.
Password managers can help users create and manage unique passwords.
MFA adds another layer of account protection.
Passwords and MFA codes should not be casually shared.
Credential theft can occur through phishing, fake login pages, social engineering, malware, and other methods.
Account takeover occurs when an unauthorized person gains control of an account.
Password-reset messages should be verified carefully.
Primary email and other high-value accounts deserve stronger protection.
Password-strength tools should educate users without permanently storing passwords.
For training tools, users should test fictional passwords, not real credentials.

sections.title: 26. Reflect & Apply
sections.content: Think about your own account-security habits:
bulletPoints: Which of your accounts are most important?
Do your important accounts use unique passwords?
Is MFA enabled on your primary email?
Do you know how to recognize an unexpected password-reset scam?
Do you know what you would do if someone gained access to one of your accounts?
Are your account-recovery methods still current?
sections.callout: Before moving to the next module, you should be able to explain: Strong Passwords, Unique Credentials, Password Managers, MFA, Credential Protection, and Account Takeover Prevention.

interactiveExercises.title: Password Strength Checker
interactiveExercises.instruction: Use the Password Strength Checker to test various passwords and see how factors like length and character variety affect the strength.

interactiveExercises.title: Build a Better Account
interactiveExercises.question: You are setting up a new professional account. Which combination offers the best security?
options: A long passphrase used only for this account + MFA.
The same password you use for your social media.
A password written on a sticky note on your monitor.
interactiveExercises.correctAnswer: A long passphrase used only for this account + MFA.
interactiveExercises.explanation: Combining uniqueness, length, and MFA provides the highest level of protection.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected MFA Alert
scenarios.content: Your phone buzzes with a verification code you didn't request, followed by a call from someone claiming to be 'IT Support' asking for the code.
scenarios.action: Do NOT share the code. IT will never ask for your MFA code or password. This is a credential theft attempt.
scenarios.lesson: MFA codes are private and should never be shared.

choices.text: Read the code aloud to the caller — they said they are IT
choices.consequence: You handed the attacker the second factor. Combined with a leaked password they may already have, they can now log into your account from their own device.

choices.text: Hang up and call IT back on the official number listed on your intranet / ID badge
choices.consequence: You broke the attacker's live session. A callback on a number you already trust confirms whether a real support case exists — IT will never ask for your MFA code.

choices.text: Make up a fake code and give it to them to waste their time
choices.consequence: You are still engaged with a social engineer. They may try a different tactic on the same call, pressure you harder, or move on to another colleague in your organization.

choices.text: Text the code to a friend to ask what to do
choices.consequence: The code is now in an unprotected message thread and visible to anyone with access to that phone. MFA codes should never leave your authenticator app.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Hang up and call IT back on the official number listed on your intranet / ID badge
scenarios.securityPrinciple: Never share MFA codes or passwords with anyone claiming to be support — real IT will never ask for them.

scenarios.title: Urgent Deletion Warning
scenarios.content: You receive an email: 'Your account will be deleted in 10 minutes unless you click here to verify your identity.'
scenarios.lesson: Scammers use fear and urgency to make you act without thinking.

choices.text: Click the link quickly before the account is deleted
choices.consequence: The link leads to a phishing page designed to harvest your credentials. Real services do not threaten instant deletion in an email.

choices.text: Reply asking for proof that the account is real
choices.consequence: You confirm to the attacker that your mailbox is active and responsive, which puts you on a higher-value target list for future scams.

choices.text: Ignore the email and log into the service directly through its official website or app
choices.consequence: If there is a real issue, it will be visible inside the authenticated account. You bypass the email's urgency and verify through a trusted channel.

choices.text: Forward the email to coworkers to warn them
choices.consequence: Forwarding spreads the malicious link. Some recipients may click before anyone realizes it is a scam.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Ignore the email and log into the service directly through its official website or app
scenarios.securityPrinciple: Treat urgency and threats as attack tools; verify by logging in through the service's official site or app.

scenarios.title: Unrecognized Device Login
scenarios.content: You receive a legitimate alert from a service stating: 'New login detected from a Linux device in another country.'
scenarios.action: Immediately change your password and check for unauthorized changes to the account.
scenarios.lesson: Login alerts are a critical early warning system for account takeover.

choices.text: Dismiss the alert — you probably logged in from somewhere and forgot
choices.consequence: If the login is not yours, the attacker now has an active session. Ignoring the alert is the difference between stopping a takeover in minutes and discovering it in months.

choices.text: Log into the service directly (not via the alert), change your password, and review recent activity
choices.consequence: You cut off the attacker's current session, lock out anyone with your old password, and create an audit trail the service can use to investigate.

choices.text: Reply to the alert email asking for more information
choices.consequence: If the alert email is spoofed or part of a phishing chain, your reply hands an active conversation to the attacker.

choices.text: Share the alert on social media to get advice
choices.consequence: You expose details about your accounts and the incident. Attackers monitoring your profile can use those details to refine their next attempt.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Log into the service directly (not via the alert), change your password, and review recent activity
scenarios.securityPrinciple: Act on login alerts immediately through the service directly — early warnings stop account takeover in minutes, not months.

tools.name: Have I Been Pwned
tools.description: A website that allows you to check if your email address or phone number has been compromised in a known data breach.

quiz.question: Which of these is the MOST important factor for a strong password?
quiz.explanation: Length significantly increases the time it takes for automated tools to crack a password.

quiz.question: Is it safe to use the same password for your bank account and your favorite pizza shop's loyalty app?
quiz.explanation: Password reuse is a major risk. If the pizza shop has a breach, your bank account is now vulnerable.

quiz.question: What does MFA stand for?
quiz.explanation: MFA requires two or more pieces of evidence to verify a user's identity.

quiz.question: A password manager is useful because:
options: It lets you write passwords on paper.
It stores all your unique passwords in one secure place.
It makes you use '123456' for everything.
It shares your passwords with friends.
quiz.correctAnswer: It stores all your unique passwords in one secure place.
quiz.explanation: It helps maintain unique, strong passwords without needing to memorize them all.

quiz.question: What should you do if someone from 'IT' calls and asks for your MFA code to 'fix your account'?
options: Ask them to wait while you find it.
Refuse to give the code and hang up.
Email the code to them instead.
quiz.correctAnswer: Refuse to give the code and hang up.
quiz.explanation: Legitimate IT staff will never ask for your password or MFA code.

quiz.question: Which is an example of 'something you are' in MFA?
Credential theft occurs when:
options: Your computer runs out of battery.
An attacker steals your username and password.
quiz.correctAnswer: An attacker steals your username and password.
quiz.explanation: Stealing login details is the primary goal of credential theft.

quiz.question: Why are common passwords like '123456' dangerous?
options: They are the first ones attackers try using automated software.
quiz.correctAnswer: They are the first ones attackers try using automated software.
quiz.explanation: Attackers use lists of common passwords to easily compromise accounts.

keyTakeaways: Use long, unique passphrases for every account.
Use a password manager to handle unique credentials safely.
Never share MFA codes or passwords with anyone, even 'IT'.
reflectApply: Which of your accounts (Email, Bank, Social Media) currently lack MFA? Can you enable it today?
Check your most important accounts. Are any of them using the same password?
